context: Current closing price of Costco (COST): $942.06 USD as of 2026-08-05.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 944 was anchored heavily on the most recent observed price level, assuming mean-reverting behavior and little directional catalyst in the immediate term. At one week, the slight uptick to 948 reflects a small positive drift assumption built into the random walk framework, acknowledging that markets tend to carry modest momentum over short periods. By one month, the estimate nudges to 955, incorporating slightly more drift while still staying close to current levels, as the compounding of daily drift over roughly 20 trading sessions produces only a modest displacement from the starting point.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by historical volatility of the underlying asset. At one day, the interval is fairly tight — roughly plus or minus 22 points — reflecting the relatively limited range of typical daily price moves. As the horizon extends to one week, the uncertainty fans out to approximately plus or minus 43 points, scaled by the square root of time as one would expect under standard diffusion assumptions. By one month, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus 85 points, capturing the accumulated uncertainty from compounding daily variance over many sessions. I also factored in some additional uncertainty beyond pure statistical volatility, acknowledging that realized distributions of asset prices tend to have fatter tails than a normal distribution would suggest.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden risk-off event — such as a sharp deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift, or a geopolitical shock — could drive prices significantly below the lower bound. Liquidity-driven selloffs can produce moves that far exceed what historical volatility would predict, particularly over the one-week and one-month horizons. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as better-than-expected earnings data, a dovish policy surprise, or a resolution of a major geopolitical uncertainty could push prices well above the upper bound.

Finally, structural regime changes pose the greatest threat to the validity of all three intervals simultaneously. If the underlying asset were to enter a new volatility regime — either much calmer or much more turbulent than recent history — the interval widths themselves would be miscalibrated, not just the point estimates. Model risk of this kind is difficult to quantify but is real, and readers should treat these intervals as reflecting a baseline scenario conditioned on conditions remaining broadly similar to recent history rather than as hard probabilistic guarantees.
